After reading the scenario, please respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe how selective incorporation applies to this scenario and explain how that process impacted the Mapp v. Ohio decision.
  2. Explain how state legislatures could minimize the impact of the Court’s decision in Mapp v. Ohio.
  3. Describe how due process relates to the scenario and explain how changes in the membership of the Court could affect future rulings on this constitutional protection.

f.c:
Laws and rules governing searches and seizures by the police or other government agents stem from the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution. During the nineteenth century search warrants became a way to limit police authority. In the 1914 U.S. Supreme Court case Weeks v. United States, the Court determined that “where letters and papers of the accused were taken from . . . premises by an official of the United States . . . without any search warrant,” a violation of constitutional protections had occurred.

In 1957, Cleveland police officers forcibly entered the home of Dollree Mapp and conducted a warrantless search for a bombing suspect. Although no suspect was found, officers discovered allegedly obscene materials, the possession of which was prohibited under Ohio state law. Mapp was later convicted of possessing obscene materials. She appealed her conviction on the basis that the officers admitted to using a false warrant and the confiscated materials were protected from seizure by the Fourth Amendment.

In 1961, the Supreme Court ruled in Mapp v. Ohio that the exclusionary rule, which prevents prosecutors from using evidence in court obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment, applied in Mapp’s case because the Ohio police officers had obtained the evidence illegally.

q.s:
After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the foundation of the authority of the DEA to carry out the Prescription Drug Marketing Act and explain how the president could affect the powers of the DEA.
  2. Explain how congressional oversight of the DEA in this scenario reflects the principle of checks and balances.
  3. Describe what the Supreme Court could do if a case with a question about the Prescription Drug Marketing Act came before the Court. Explain how the actions of the Court could impact the ability of the DEA to carry out its efforts to eliminate drug trafficking and distribution.

f.c:
The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is the federal law enforcement agency under the Department of Justice that is tasked with eliminating drug trafficking and distribution. One of the many laws that they enforce is the Prescription Drug Marketing Act, passed in 1987. This act established safe guidelines for distributing prescription drugs and discouraged the sale of counterfeit drugs.

By the late 1990s, there was a rising epidemic in the abuse of a wide category of pain relief drugs. By 2005, the DEA realized traditional enforcement against individual doctors and pharmacies was no longer effective and they began to investigate drug wholesale companies. These companies were distributing hundreds of millions of highly addictive prescription medications to doctors, clinics, and pharmacies. DEA investigators filed civil cases against questionable distributors, issued orders to suspend the flow of drugs and, in some cases, imposed fines. In 2011, there were 131 civil court filings against distributors, manufacturers, pharmacies, and doctors.

In response to this increase in the prosecution of drug wholesale companies, representatives of the pharmaceutical industry and some members of Congress worked to create a new law that would require a higher standard of proof from investigators before cases could move forward. As a result, the number of case filings dropped to 40 in 2014.

After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the foundation of the authority of OSHA to carry out policy regarding working conditions and explain how the federal courts can influence OSHA’s authority.
  2. Referencing the scenario, explain how the ideology of the president may influence the powers of OSHA.
  3. Describe an action Congress could take to provide oversight for OSHA in this scenario and explain how divided government might impact Congress’s ability to oversee OSHA.

f.c:
When Republican George W. Bush became president in 2001, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) issued the fewest regulations in the history of the federal agency. This agency was created by an act of Congress in 1970. Its main task has been to ensure safe and healthy working conditions for working men and women in the private sector.

According to a 2007 New York Times report, the agency had eliminated dozens of existing and proposed regulations and delayed adopting others. Experts who researched the Bush administration said OSHA had imposed only one major rule between 2001 and 2007.

Instead of regulations, the director of OSHA, Edwin Foulke, said that they and other agencies favor a “voluntary compliance strategy,” reaching agreements with industry associations and companies to police themselves. He also said that he “firmly believes in limited government.” When the Democrats took control of Congress in 2007, they vowed to increase oversight of OSHA.

After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the foundation of the power that the EPA exercised related to the Clean Water Act, and explain how the EPA’s power can have an impact on civil liberties.
  2. Explain why a political appointee, such as the head of the EPA, might implement changes to the Clean Water Act differently than the civil servants who work within the EPA.
  3. Describe an informal power the president could use to influence the EPA’s policies regarding the Clean Water Act, and explain how the president’s statement might impact the actions of the EPA.

f.c:
The Clean Water Act is a federal law that was established in 1972 to regulate the discharge of pollutants into the country’s surface waters, including lakes, streams, rivers, wetlands, and coastal areas. In 2015, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) finalized a policy under the Clean Water Act that regulated water on private property. This policy, called the “Waters of the United States,” defined which bodies of water were subject to the protections of the Clean Water Act, including wetlands, ponds on private property, and streams.

The EPA made this change as it argued that the connection between these waters and larger bodies of water, like lakes, rivers, and larger streams, meant that pollution in these smaller waters needed to be regulated. Many of the bodies of water regulated under the Waters of the United States rule existed on private property, giving the EPA the ability to inspect these waters to ensure that individuals, farmers, or businesses were complying with the Clean Water Act.

The president issued a reversal of this rule in 2019. In a statement, the president said that he did not want the government to manage water on private land, stating that this reversal will keep EPA inspectors from being able to tell individuals and businesses how to operate on their property.

After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the foundation of the power that the FAA exercised related to the use of personal electronic devices, and explain how the president can affect the FAA’s power.
  2. Explain why civil servants working within the FAA might implement changes to federal law described in the scenario differently than a political appointee, such as the head of the FAA.
  3. Describe an action Congress could take if they have concerns about the policy changes described in the scenario, and explain how their action could impact the authority of the FAA to influence federal policies related to airline safety.

f.c:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), a division of the U.S. Department of Transportation, regulates most aspects of airline travel in the United States. One portion of the FAA’s mission is maintaining the safety of airline travel. In 2013, the FAA announced that it would allow passengers to use personal electronic devices, including cell phones, e-readers, and tablets, during all phases of travel if the device remained in airplane mode. This change permitted passengers to watch videos, read, or play games on their devices as long as they were not using these devices for voice communication, such as phone calls.

The FAA made this change after it determined that commercial airplanes could operate safely without electronic interference from these personal electronic devices. The FAA also worked with interest groups, unions, and corporations, including those who represent flight attendants, pilots, airline manufacturers, and passengers, to ensure these groups supported the new policy.

After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the informal power being used by President Bush and explain how that power might impact the actions of the secretary of energy.
  2. In the context of the scenario, explain how the bureaucracy might hinder cooperation among the Department of Transportation, the Department of Energy, and the Environmental Protection Agency.
  3. Describe an action the legislative branch could take to affect how the bureaucracy is implementing President Bush’s order. Explain how partisanship in Congress could slow legislative action on the issue highlighted in the scenario.

f.c:
Throughout his second term, President George W. Bush proposed initiatives aimed at decreasing greenhouse gas emissions and protecting the environment. Among President Bush’s proposals were issuing standards to decrease the amount of gasoline cars consume per mile and utilizing cleaner energy technologies.

On January 24, 2007, President Bush ordered bureaucratic agencies to reduce greenhouse gases through listing requirements such as sustainable environmental practices, including the purchase of bio-based, energy efficient, water efficient, and recycled content products, and buying electric or hybrid vehicles. Federal agencies would also need to ensure that at least half of current renewable energy would come from solar, wind, or other renewable sources.

On May 14, 2007, President Bush issued an order calling for the Department of Transportation, the Department of Energy, and the Environmental Protection Agency to cooperate with respect to greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles “in a manner consistent with sound science, analysis of benefits and cost, public safety, and economic growth.” The intent of the order was to streamline bureaucratic implementation of environmental policy and foster cooperation between the agencies.

After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the informal power being used by President Reagan and explain how the president’s action reflects the principle of federalism.
  2. In the context of the scenario, explain how the bureaucracy could impact the implementation of President Reagan’s order.
  3. Describe an action the legislative branch could take to respond to President Reagan’s order. Explain why Democratic control in Congress might make this action more likely against President Reagan’s order.

f.c:
On October 26, 1987, Republican President Ronald Reagan issued an order expressing his desire “to restore the division of governmental responsibilities between the national government and the States that was intended by the Framers of the Constitution.” This order was issued to “guide the Executive departments and agencies in the formulation and implementation of policies. . . that [had] substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.”

The action by the president contained several directives to federal agencies. These directives included telling the agencies not to establish uniform national standards unless it was absolutely necessary and even then, to be sure and consult with the appropriate state officials in developing those standards. The president also told executive departments not to ask Congress for legislation that would regulate the states or override existing state laws if at all possible.

After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the informal power being used by the president and explain how the use of that power can influence the legislative process.
  2. Explain how the partisan control of Congress described in this scenario impacted the passage of the First Step Act.
  3. Describe another part of the executive branch, other than the president, that could affect this legislation after its passage. Explain how that part of the executive branch might affect the success of the First Step Act after its passage.

f.c:
Republicans won control of the Senate in the 2014 elections, resulting in a Republican majority in both chambers of Congress. With a win in the presidential elections of 2016, the Republicans were now in charge of a unified government. One part of the Republican party platform emphasized law and order, including tougher sentences for those convicted of crimes. In 2016, the attorney general directed federal prosecutors to bring the most serious charges possible against federal defendants, a shift in direction from the previous administration.

However, in January of 2018, the president attended a roundtable session that addressed growing concerns about the prison system. Justice Department statistics show that about two-thirds of the 650,000 people who leave the corrections system every year are arrested again within three years. On May 7, 2018, a bill called the First Step Act was introduced into the House of Representatives. The First Step Act sought to address the high rearrest rate cited at the January 2018 roundtable by introducing a series of prison reforms. The president used the power of his office to support this bill and promoted its merits in the media. The legislation passed the House with strong support from both parties. In the Senate, it faced a tougher battle, but the president continued to pressure for passage of the bill. The Senate eventually passed the legislation and the First Step Act became law on December 21, 2018.

q.s:
After reading the scenario, respond to A, B, and C below.

  1. Referencing the scenario, describe the executive branch authority used by the FDA in reclassifying insulin as a biologic and explain how this use of the FDA’s authority might affect the success of the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act.
  2. Referencing the scenario, explain how Congress could have addressed the increasing cost of insulin prior to 2017.
  3. Describe an informal power the president could use to influence the FDA’s decision to reclassify insulin as a biologic. Explain how the use of that informal power relates to the principle of separation of powers.

f.c:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is the federal agency responsible for the approval, regulation, and control of prescription medications. All prescription medications must complete an extensive FDA approval process, which can take years. In an attempt to expedite this process, Congress passed the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act in 2009, which created a faster approval pathway for biologic products that are highly similar to existing FDA-approved medications. The law applies only to biologic products, those produced with living organisms, but not to chemically produced drugs. Insulin is a vital prescription medication used to treat diabetes. Over an eight-year period, beginning in 2009, the average price of insulin increased from $90 to $275 a vial. Since insulin was not regulated as a biologic, the time necessary to gain FDA approval prevented new companies from developing less expensive alternatives.

In 2017, public attention to the rising cost of insulin led the FDA to reclassify the drug as a biologic, thereby lessening the amount of time it took for new companies to get FDA approval. With more manufacturers competing in the marketplace, prices would likely drop.

An iron triangle is a stable, mutually beneficial relationship among three key actors in policymaking: a congressional committee, a bureaucratic agency, and an interest group or industry. In option i3, the energy industry lobbyists (interest group), the Department of Energy (bureaucratic agency), and the House Energy and Commerce Committee (congressional committee) form this classic three-way relationship. The lobbyists provide information and expertise to the agency, the agency implements policies favorable to the industry, and the committee oversees the agency while receiving campaign support from the industry. This scenario demonstrates all three components of an iron triangle working together in a specific policy area.

q.s: A 2013 YouGov poll question asked, “President Obama says the 1975 Public Affairs Act should be repealed. Do you agree or disagree?” The results showed that 13 percent of Democrats agreed and 39 percent of Republicans disagreed. However, the 1975 Public Affairs Act is fictitious. Which of the following is illustrated by the scenario?

o.l: The type of information given in a poll question can affect how individuals respond.
Public opinion polls can serve as a source of public support for elected officials.
Sampling techniques that use small sample sizes usually produce more reliable results.
When the question wording is accurate, there is no margin of error.

q.ex: The scenario demonstrates that respondents often react to cues within poll questions rather than their actual knowledge of the subject matter. Since the 1975 Public Affairs Act does not exist, respondents who agreed or disagreed were influenced by the framing element that "President Obama says" it should be repealed, triggering partisan responses rather than informed opinions. Democrats were more likely to support what Obama allegedly supported, while Republicans were more likely to oppose it, despite neither group having any actual knowledge of the nonexistent act. This illustrates how the type of information presented in a poll question—in this case, associating a position with a political figure—can significantly affect how individuals respond.

Name recognition is a crucial factor because voters are more likely to support candidates they have heard of or seen in office. This visibility creates familiarity and trust that challengers struggle to overcome, even with substantial campaign efforts. The correct answer is that incumbents have an advantage over challengers because of name recognition, as this fundamental benefit directly explains why sitting members of Congress consistently win reelection at rates typically exceeding 90 percent in the House of Representatives.

A citizen serves on a jury and receives training on how to apply the law.
A suspect is informed of his rights by an officer who is about to interrogate him.

q.ex: Political socialization is the process by which individuals acquire their political beliefs, values, and attitudes through various influences in their environment. The family is widely recognized as the primary agent of political socialization, especially during childhood and adolescence. When a teenager hears her parents discussing politics at the dinner table and this influences her own views, this directly demonstrates the transmission of political attitudes from one generation to the next through family interaction. The other options describe government policies or legal procedures but do not illustrate the developmental process of forming political beliefs. Option i2 is correct because it shows the fundamental mechanism of political socialization through family influence.

This creates a federal system where states serve as a crucial foundation and check against potential federal tyranny. The correct answer reflects Madison's view that states have structural advantages in resisting federal encroachment, making them the base upon which the federal system rests rather than merely subordinate entities.

Option i3 is correct because the 45-54 age group's voter turnout rate is positioned closest to the overall

q.s: Which of the following is most likely an effect of the data reported in the chart?

o.l: Younger voters were more likely to vote in the 2016 presidential election.
The California state government is more likely to address issues that affect older voters.
Political parties will work to recruit more younger candidates to run for office.

VOTER TURNOUT BY AGE, 2014 CALIFORNIA GENERAL ELECTION

Source: California Secretary of State, 2014

q.ex: The data in the chart most likely shows voter turnout rates by age group, with older voters participating at higher rates than younger voters. When certain demographic groups vote at higher rates, elected officials and government institutions are more responsive to their policy preferences and concerns because politicians seek to appeal to reliable voters who can help them win elections. Since older Californians vote more consistently, the California state government has a strong electoral incentive to prioritize issues important to senior citizens, such as Social Security, Medicare, and retirement security. q.s: Which of the following activities by interest groups best illustrates attempts to educate members of Congress on public policy?

o.l: A green energy group sending a research report to congressional offices
A law-reform group sending alerts to its members encouraging them to contact their representatives
A single-issue group holding a rally in Washington to show support for their cause
A PAC giving contributions to the reelection campaigns of members of Congress

q.ex: Interest groups educate members of Congress by providing information, research, and expertise on policy issues to help legislators make informed decisions. Sending a research report directly to congressional offices represents a direct educational effort, as it supplies lawmakers with data and analysis on green energy policy. The other options illustrate different lobbying tactics: mobilizing grassroots pressure through member alerts, demonstrating public support through rallies, and providing financial support through campaign contributions. While these activities may influence Congress, they do not primarily serve an educational function of informing legislators about policy details and implications. A green energy group sending a research report is correct because it directly provides substantive policy information to educate congressional decision-makers.

q.s: Which of the following explains the constitutional reasoning in McDonald v. Chicago (2010) ?

o.l: The equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires Congress to protect an individual’s ability to keep and bear arms under the Second Amendment.
The Second Amendment is a collective right and not one intended for individual application.
The full faith and credit clause requires the state of Illinois to respect the laws of neighboring states concerning the right to keep and bear arms.
The Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms for the purpose of self-defense is applicable to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

q.ex:
McDonald v. Chicago (2010) applied the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms to state and local governments through the doctrine of selective incorporation via the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause. The Supreme Court determined that the right to keep and bear arms for self-defense is a fundamental right that is deeply rooted in American history and tradition. Through selective incorporation, this fundamental right became binding on the states, not just the federal government. The Court specifically emphasized that the purpose of self-defense is central to the Second Amendment right and that this protection extends to state action through the Fourteenth Amendment.

The correct choice is i4 because it accurately describes the Court's reasoning

q.s: Which of the following is an example of a power exclusively granted to the Senate in Article II of the Constitution?

o.l: Declaring war
Overriding a presidential veto with a two-thirds majority veto
Confirming ambassadors
Creating spending bills

q.ex: Article II of the Constitution establishes the executive branch and outlines the appointment powers of the President, which require Senate approval. The Senate has the exclusive constitutional power to provide "advice and consent" on presidential appointments, including ambassadors, Supreme Court justices, and other federal officials. This power is not shared with the House of Representatives, making it a Senate-exclusive function. Declaring war is a power of Congress as a whole, overriding vetoes requires both chambers, and spending bills must originate in the House, so none of these are Senate-exclusive powers. Confirming ambassadors is correct because it is specifically granted to the Senate alone under Article II, Section 2

q.s: Which of the following statements draws an accurate comparison from the information graphic?

o.l: The Nixon “Boomer” generation was far more likely to vote Democrat when they were eighteen year olds than the Truman “Silent” generation.
The Ford/Carter “Boomer” generation has voted more consistently Republican than has the Bush/Obama “Millennial” generation.
The Roosevelt “Greatest” generation voted Democrat in 2000 but voted Republican in 2006.

q.ex: The correct answer requires comparing voting patterns across generations shown in the information graphic. The Ford/Carter Boomers demonstrate more consistent Republican voting behavior over time compared to the Bush/Obama Millennials, whose voting patterns show greater variation between Democratic and Republican candidates across election cycles. Consistency in voting refers to how reliably a generation supports one party over multiple elections. The graphic evidently shows the Ford/Carter Boomers maintaining steadier Republican preferences while Millennials display more fluctuation in their party support. This makes option i2 the accurate comparison because it correctly identifies the relative consistency of Republican voting between these two generational cohorts based on the data presented.

q.s: Which of the following serves as an explanation for the differences between generations in voting patterns?

o.l: Regional political party realignment
Shifting issue networks
Major political events affecting political attitudes
Changes in political party mobilization techniques

q.ex: Generational differences in voting patterns are primarily explained by major political events that shape the political attitudes of individuals during their formative years. Events such as the Great Depression, World War II, the Vietnam War, or the 2008 financial crisis create lasting impressions on young voters that influence their political views throughout their lives. This phenomenon, known as political socialization, means that each generation develops distinct political perspectives based on the significant events they experienced during their youth. While regional realignments, issue networks, and mobilization techniques can affect voting patterns, they do not specifically explain why different age cohorts consistently vote differently across time. Major political events affecting political attitudes is correct because it directly addresses

This passage establishes the principle of judicial review, which allows courts to evaluate whether laws conform to constitutional requirements. Marbury v. Madison (1803) is the landmark case in which Chief Justice John Marshall established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review, asserting that it is the duty of the judicial branch to interpret the Constitution and declare laws unconstitutional when they conflict with it. q.s: Which of the following best matches a political ideology with that ideology’s position on the proper role of government in regulating the economy?

o.l: Communitarian—The government should regulate monetary policy but not fiscal policy.
Libertarian—Government regulation should increase when the economy is in decline.
Conservative—The government should strictly limit its regulation of the marketplace.
Liberal—The government should not intervene in economic decision-making.

q.ex: Conservatism in American politics traditionally emphasizes free-market capitalism and limited government intervention in the economy. Conservatives generally believe that market forces, rather than government regulation, should determine economic outcomes and that excessive regulation stifles economic growth and individual liberty. This philosophy aligns with the principle that the government should strictly limit its regulation of the marketplace, allowing businesses to operate with minimal interference. In contrast, liberals typically favor more government regulation, libertarians oppose nearly all economic intervention, and communitarians focus on balancing individual rights with community needs rather than distinguishing between monetary and fiscal policy regulation. Option i3 is correct because it accurately reflects the conservative ideology's core belief in minimal government

Voting restrictions are needed to prevent voter fraud.
Voting restrictions help reduce the cost of elections.
Voting restrictions increase the accuracy of tracking polls.

This argument centers on the idea that requiring voter identification, limiting early voting periods, or restricting mail-in ballots helps ensure only eligible voters cast ballots and that each person votes only once. While opponents argue that documented cases of voter fraud are extremely rare and that such restrictions disproportionately affect minority and low-income voters, proponents maintain that preventing fraud—even if uncommon—is essential to preserving public confidence in electoral outcomes. The other options do not represent the primary rationale used by voting restriction advocates, as their central claim focuses on election

q.s: Based on the map above, a prediction that could be made about the 2016 election in Texas (TX) is that

the number of eligible voters decreased in the 2016 election

the electoral college vote was split between Democrats and Republicans

A decrease in eligible voters could result from factors such as population migration, changes in citizenship status, or shifts in age demographics that affect voting eligibility. q.s: Which of the following best reflects a function of the Supreme Court in Article III of the Constitution?

o.l: To interpret the constitutionality of laws passed by Congress
To adjudicate disputes between the president and Congress
To overturn legislation passed by the state legislatures
To serve as the highest court of appeals

q.ex: Article III of the Constitution establishes the judicial branch and defines the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction and appellate jurisdiction. The Constitution explicitly states that the Supreme Court shall have appellate jurisdiction over cases arising under federal law, with such exceptions as Congress may make. While the Supreme Court does interpret constitutionality and resolve disputes, these functions developed through practice and precedent rather than being explicitly stated in Article III. The text of Article III most directly establishes the Supreme Court as the highest court in the federal judiciary with the power to review decisions from lower courts. Therefore, serving as the highest court of appeals is the function most clearly reflected in the constitutional text itself.

q.s: Which of the following exemplifies the free-rider problem for interest groups?

A teacher who does not join the union but still receives the salary and benefits negotiated by the union is a classic example of free-riding, as the teacher enjoys the fruits of collective bargaining without bearing any of the costs of union membership. As the population has grown and demand for these services has increased, state and local governments have needed to hire more employees to meet these needs. This growth in state and local employment reflects the fundamental structure of American federalism, where subnational governments play a crucial role in providing direct services to citizens.

q.s: Which of the following is an effect of the Seventeenth Amendment?

Suffrage for women greatly expanded in national elections.

q.ex:
The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, changed the method of selecting United States senators from appointment by state legislatures to direct election by the voters of each state. This constitutional change was part of the Progressive Era reforms aimed at increasing democratic participation and reducing corruption in the political process. Prior to this amendment, senators were chosen by state legislators, which often led to political deals and limited citizen involvement in selecting their federal representatives. The amendment explicitly states that senators shall be elected by the people of each state, thereby expanding direct democracy at the federal level.

The correct answer is i2 because the Seventeenth Amendment specifically enabled people to participate in the political process by directly

q.s: Which of the following accurately describes the composition of congressional committees?

o.l: Committees are organized by the executive branch to ensure that both branches can communicate and negotiate policy goals.
The United States Constitution requires that Congress organize itself into committees, with each party having equal access to committee seats.
Committees are organized by the majority party to maintain control of the policy-making process.
Committees are organized by state delegations so that each state has some role in deciding which bills get passed.

q.ex: Congressional committees are organized and controlled by the majority party in each chamber of Congress. The majority party holds more seats on each committee proportional to their overall numbers in the chamber and selects all committee chairs, giving them significant power over the legislative agenda. This organizational structure allows the majority party to control which bills receive hearings, which amendments are considered, and which legislation advances to the floor for a vote. The Constitution does not mandate equal party representation on committees, committees are not organized by the executive branch, and they are not structured by state delegations. Option i3 is correct because the majority party uses its numerical advantage to organize committees in a way that maintains its control over the policy-making

Option i1 correctly pairs these two accountability mechanisms. The other options either list actions that are not primarily oversight tools, such as negotiating treaties or meeting in caucuses, or include powers that Congress does not possess, such as firing civil servants who are protected by civil service laws.

q.s: Which of the following is an accurate comparison of an exit poll and a tracking poll?

o.l:
Exit PollTracking Poll
The poll is conducted immediately after voting occurs.Nonrandom sampling techniques are used to choose respondents to take part in the poll.

Exit PollTracking Poll
Respondents are assembled to participate in a discussion led by the polling company.Tracking polls are used to gauge presidential approval ratings over time.

Exit PollTracking Poll
The poll allows both voters and nonvoters to participate.The poll is conducted in a way that does not ensure that the opinions are representative of the larger population.

Exit PollTracking Poll
Responses can be used to judge election results before the official count is obtained.The poll is conducted over time to obtain information about changes in public opinion.

q.ex: An exit poll is conducted as voters leave polling places on election day, asking them how they voted. This allows media organizations and analysts to project election outcomes before official vote tallies are complete. A tracking poll is a survey conducted repeatedly over a period of time, using the same or similar questions to measure how public opinion shifts on particular issues or candidates. Option i4 correctly identifies that exit polls can predict election results before official counts are finalized, while tracking polls measure changes in opinion over time. This is the correct choice because it accurately captures the defining purpose of each polling method.

q.s: Which of the following is a correct comparison of formal and informal powers of the president?

o.l:
Formal PowerInformal Power
Delivering the State of the Union to CongressIssuing a pardon to a person convicted of a federal crime

Formal PowerInformal Power
Negotiating treaties with leaders of other nationsAppointing ambassadors and receiving diplomats from other nations

Formal PowerInformal Power
Using the veto to block legislationIssuing executive orders to bureaucratic agencies without having to gain approval from Congress

Formal PowerInformal Power
Using executive privilege to withhold information from CongressUsing signing statements to interpret various provisions of legislation

q.ex: Formal powers are those explicitly granted to the president by the Constitution, while informal powers are those derived from custom, tradition, or interpretation rather than explicit constitutional text. The veto power is explicitly stated in Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution, making it a formal power. Executive orders, while having legal force, are not mentioned in the Constitution and have evolved through practice and judicial interpretation as a way for presidents to direct the executive branch, making them an informal power. Option i3 correctly categorizes the veto as formal and executive orders as informal, distinguishing between constitutionally enumerated authority and powers that have developed through presidential practice.

Both statements in option i1 accurately reflect these fundamental procedural differences between the chambers. o.l: Pluralist

The scenario describes multiple competing interest groups contacting members of Congress through various channels to advocate for their preferred policies, which directly illustrates the core mechanism of pluralist democracy. The politico and trustee options refer to models of legislative representation rather than models of democracy, while the elitist model would involve a small group of powerful actors controlling policy rather than many competing groups. q.s: Which of the following is the best summary of the author’s argument?

o.l: The expansion of democracy is seen as the primary cause of political conflict in the world.
The world is becoming more globally united but also more aware of cultural differences, which may lead to conflict.
The threat of terrorism requires cooperation, which is nearly impossible to achieve.
Consumers in other parts of the world are less excited about American commercial products such as MTV, Macintosh, and McDonald’s.

f.c:
Just beyond the horizon of current events lie two possible political futures—both bleak, neither democratic. The first is a retribalization of large swaths of humankind by war and bloodshed: a threatened Lebanonization of national states in which culture is pitted against culture, people against people, tribe against tribe—a Jihad in the name of a hundred narrowly conceived faiths against every kind of interdependence, every kind of artificial social cooperation and civic mutuality. The second is being borne in on us by the onrush of economic and ecological forces that demand integration and uniformity and that mesmerize the world with fast music, fast computers, and fast food—with MTV, Macintosh, and McDonald’s, pressing nations into one commercially homogeneous global network: one McWorld tied together by technology, ecology, communications, and commerce. The planet is falling precipitantly apart and coming reluctantly together at the very same moment.

Benjamin Barber, “Jihad vs. McWorld,” 1992

q.ex:
The correct answer identifies a paradox of globalization where increased interconnectedness occurs simultaneously with heightened awareness of cultural distinctions. This reflects a central tension in contemporary international relations where economic and technological integration brings societies closer together while simultaneously making populations more conscious of their unique cultural identities and differences. The argument suggests this dual process creates potential for conflict as groups assert their distinctiveness even as global forces push toward uniformity. This best captures the nuanced relationship between global unity and cultural awareness that characterizes modern political dynamics.

The correct choice is i2 because it accurately summarizes the author's argument about the simultaneous trends of global integration and cultural differentiation leading to potential conflict.

This reflects the broader phenomenon of American cultural and economic values spreading beyond U.S. borders through various channels including multinational corporations, international financial institutions, and diplomatic relationships. The correct answer is i1 because it accurately recognizes that free market principles, which are central to American political culture, have indeed influenced the political and economic cultures of other countries worldwide.

This landmark decision held that while race can be considered as one factor in redistricting, it cannot be the predominant factor without compelling justification. q.ex:

Conservative Republican candidates successfully won seats previously held by conservative Democrats, effectively replacing them in Southern congressional delegations. q.s: A classified Department of Defense study on the effectiveness of the United States involvement in the Afghanistan War is obtained by a newspaper. The president seeks to block the publication of the document. The court rules in favor of the newspaper, citing as precedent the Supreme Court’s decision in New York Times Co. v. United States (1971). Based on the ruling in the Supreme Court’s decision, which of the following lines of reasoning does the court most likely use?

o.l: Freedom of the press cannot be abridged except for restrictions on time, place, and manner of the communication.
Freedom of the press requires that the government show a significant danger to national security in order to stop publication.
Freedom of the press permits the press to print any story, but if the story embarrasses public officials, they can sue under defamation laws.
Freedom of the press cannot be abridged by the actions of the president without a law passed by Congress.

q.ex: In New York Times Co. v. United States (1971), also known as the Pentagon Papers case, the Supreme Court established that prior restraint on publication requires the government to meet an extremely heavy burden of proof. The Court ruled that the government must demonstrate that publication would cause direct, immediate, and irreparable harm to the nation, such as a grave and immediate danger to national security. This creates a very high bar for the government to justify censorship before publication occurs. The correct answer reflects this principle by stating that the government must show a significant danger to national security to stop publication, which aligns with the Court's rejection of prior restraint unless extraordinary circumstances exist.

q.s: Which of the following scenarios would be considered a violation of the rights of someone accused of a crime, according to the Supreme Court?

o.l: A witness is called to testify against a suspect accused of plotting a terrorist attack.
A police officer acts to stop a crime while it is being committed but does so without a warrant.
A person who is unable to afford an attorney is tried and convicted of a crime without legal representation.
A suspect is informed of the right to an attorney but confesses to a crime prior to receiving legal advice.

q.ex: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to legal counsel in criminal prosecutions, and the Supreme Court's landmark decision in Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) established that states must provide attorneys to defendants who cannot afford them. When a person unable to afford an attorney is tried and convicted without legal representation, this directly violates their constitutional right to counsel. The other scenarios do not constitute violations: witnesses testifying is part of the Sixth Amendment right to confront witnesses, police can act without warrants in exigent circumstances or when crimes are in progress, and suspects can waive their Miranda rights and confess before receiving legal advice if the waiver is knowing

United States v. Eichman (1990)

After the Supreme Court held that a state law in Texas that criminalized the desecration of the American flag was unconstitutional, Congress passed a national law, the Flag Protection Act of 1989, which criminalized the conduct of anyone who “knowingly mutilates, defaces, physically defiles, burns, maintains on the floor or ground, or tramples upon” a flag of the United States.

In response to this law, protest demonstrations took place in several locations across the country. Several people, including Shawn Eichman, burned flags on the steps of the United States Capitol building in Washington, D.C., before a crowd of reporters and photographers. Eichman and others were arrested for violating the Flag Protection Act.

In the ensuing cases, Eichman and others defended their actions as legitimate forms of political protest. Federal district judges dismissed the charges, but United States attorneys appealed the decisions directly to the Supreme Court. These cases were consolidated in United States v. Eichman (1990).

In United States v. Eichman (1990), the Supreme Court’s 5–4 decision held that the federal government cannot prosecute a person for desecration of the American flag because doing so would violate the First Amendment.

Timbs v. Indiana (2019)

In November of 2013, Tyson Timbs was arrested after selling illegal drugs to an undercover police officer. Timbs pleaded guilty to the charges and was sentenced to a year of house arrest, five years probation, and a $1,200 fine.

In addition, the state sought to seize Timbs’s Land Rover, which Timbs used to transport the illegal drugs. The Land Rover was previously purchased for $42,000. Timbs argued that the vehicle seizure constituted an excessive fine, which was a violation of the Eighth Amendment. The maximum fine for Timbs’s crime was $10,000, which was considerably less than the price Timbs paid for the Land Rover.

In the resulting case, Timbs v. Indiana (2019), the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in favor of Timbs. The opinion of the Court, authored by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, stated that the excessive fines clause is a provision that applies to the states. The Court found that the protection against excessive fines is “fundamental to our scheme of ordered liberty” and “deeply rooted in this Nation’s history and tradition."

On September 12, 1962, President John F. Kennedy addressed a stadium crowd of 40,000 people at Rice University. The speech, officially titled “We Choose to Go to the Moon,” came just one year after the Soviet Union launched the first person into space and five years after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite into space. The purpose of the speech was to increase support for Kennedy’s proposal to launch a mission to the Moon and explain why this program needed to be a high budget priority. The event was the lead story in The New York Times and was covered in newspapers around the country.

President Kennedy talked about scientific progress and how the space mission represented a major step forward for humankind:

f.c:
This question requires you to compare a Supreme Court case you studied in class with one you have not studied in class. A summary of the Supreme Court case you did not study in class is presented below and provides all of the information you need to know about this case to answer the prompts.

 

Cantwell v. Connecticut (1940)

Newton Cantwell and his sons, who were Jehovah’s Witnesses, went door-to-door in a New Haven, Connecticut, neighborhood to distribute pamphlets about their religion and encouraged people to join their church. The men did not have a permit to solicit door-to-door. A Connecticut state court convicted the Cantwells of violating an ordinance that stated “[n]o person shall solicit money, services, subscriptions or any valuable thing for any alleged religious, charitable or philanthropic cause. . . unless such cause shall have been approved by the secretary of the public welfare council.”

Cantwell and his sons challenged the conviction, arguing that they did not need to obtain a permit because their activities were protected by the United States Constitution. The Connecticut Supreme Court upheld the conviction, finding that the statute was in the public interest and that it protected against fraud. The Cantwells appealed to the United States Supreme Court.

In a unanimous decision, the Supreme Court ruled in the Cantwells’ favor, holding that the United States Constitution prohibited states from making laws like the one in question in New Haven. The Court reasoned that the First Amendment gives citizens the right to believe, as well as the right to act on those beliefs, and regarding the right to act, laws may not deny or limit the right to preach or disseminate religious views.

f.c:
In 2003, California’s Democratic governor Gray Davis’ popularity was decreasing due to a budget shortfall and an energy crisis that received widespread coverage in the news. As a result, Republicans in the state initiated a recall election of the governor by gathering over one million signatures.

Recall is an electoral process by which citizens can vote to remove elected officials before the end of their term. There are provisions for recall elections of state officials in 19 states. In California, citizens initiate a recall election by collecting a minimum number of signatures on a petition, which puts the issue on a ballot in a subsequent election. If a majority of the voters choose to recall the elected official, then that official is removed from office. In California, the recall ballot asks voters two separate questions: Should the governor be recalled? And if so, who should be the new governor?

The front-running candidate to replace Governor Davis was action movie star Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican. Schwarzenegger announced his candidacy on a popular late-night television program, and his celebrity status drew national media attention. During his appearance, he said of Davis, “He’s failing [Californians] terribly, and this is why he needs to be recalled.” With the understanding that California had more registered Democrats than Republicans, Schwarzenegger strategically focused his campaign on his own personal story as a self-made immigrant and distanced himself from national Republican leaders.

In the final vote, Californians voted to recall Governor Davis, and Schwarzenegger was elected as his replacement. Exit polls showed that most voters who favored recalling Davis cited his recent performance as the basis for their vote.

Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002)

In response to low academic performance at public schools in lower-income sections of Cleveland, the Ohio legislature enacted a program that allowed the use of public funds for private school tuition. Parents who showed financial need could obtain vouchers of up to $2,500 a year for tuition at participating private schools. Both religious and nonreligious private schools could participate in the program, and in the first year, 96 percent of voucher recipients opted to attend religious schools.

A group of Ohio taxpayers, which included Doris Simmons-Harris, filed a lawsuit against the public school system, claiming the use of public funds for religious institutions was unconstitutional. The local federal district court ruled in favor of Simmons-Harris. After the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit upheld the ruling, Sarah Zelman, the Superintendent of Public Instruction in Ohio, appealed the ruling to the Supreme Court.

In a 5–4 vote on the subsequent case of Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002), the Supreme Court held that the public funding of a school voucher program that includes religious schools was constitutionally permitted. In the majority opinion, Chief Justice William Rehnquist reasoned that the program “. . . provides benefits directly to a wide spectrum of individuals, defined only by financial need and residence in a particular school district. It permits such individuals . . . genuine choice among options public and private, secular and religious.
